Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. Born in the Republic of Florence, he was mostly active in Rome from his 30s onwards. His work drew on models from classical antiquity and had a lasting influence on Western art. He is one of the best-documented artists of the 16th century, and with his elder rival [[Leonardo da Vinci]] he is considered an archetypal Renaissance man.

Michelangelo achieved fame early: the [[Pietà (Michelangelo)|Pietà]] and [[David (Michelangelo)|David]] were sculpted before he was 30. At 13 he was apprenticed to the painter Domenico Ghirlandaio, and from 1490 to 1492 he attended the Platonic Academy founded by the Medici. Although he did not consider himself a painter, he created two of the most influential frescoes in Western art: the scenes from Genesis on the ceiling of the [[Sistine Chapel]] (1508–12), commissioned by [[Pope Julius II]], and *The Last Judgment* (1536–41) on its altar wall. His design of the Laurentian Library pioneered Mannerist architecture. At 71 he succeeded Antonio da Sangallo the Younger as architect of [[St. Peter's Basilica]]; the western end was finished to his design, as was the dome, with some modification, after his death. He also wrote poetry, including more than 300 sonnets and madrigals.

He was the first Western artist whose biography was published during his lifetime. [[Giorgio Vasari]]'s *Lives* (1550), in which he was the only living artist given a biography, called him *divino*; Ascanio Condivi's *Life* (1553) was prepared with his participation. Contemporaries admired his *terribilità*, the ability to inspire awe. Later artists' imitation of his expressive physicality contributed to the rise of [[Mannerism]].

Branch of economics concerned with how individuals and firms make decisions about allocating scarce resources, and with the interactions among them. It focuses on individual markets, sectors, or industries, as opposed to the economy as a whole, which is studied in [[Macroeconomics]]. Macroeconomics addresses growth, [[Inflation]], and [[Unemployment]] and national policies related to them, whereas microeconomics also examines the effects of policies such as changes in [[Tax]] levels on individual behavior.

One goal of the field is to analyze the market mechanisms that establish relative prices among [[Goods]] and services and allocate limited resources among alternative uses. Historically it has been pursued through general equilibrium theory, developed by Léon Walras in *Elements of Pure Economics* (1874), and partial equilibrium theory, introduced by Alfred Marshall in *Principles of Economics* (1890). Its formal name as a distinct field emerged in the 1930s.

Theory typically begins with a single rational, utility-maximizing individual, whose rationality means stable preferences that are both complete and transitive. The utility maximization problem, a constrained optimization in which the individual maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint, is the heart of consumer theory; its solution is called a Walrasian demand function. An alternative approach, revealed preference theory, takes consumer choice as primitive.

The theory of [[Supply and demand]] usually assumes perfectly competitive markets, with many buyers and sellers, none able to influence prices significantly. Where the assumption fails, as under monopoly, more sophisticated analysis is needed. Microeconomics also analyzes [[Market failure]], in which markets produce inefficient outcomes, as with public goods. Critics question assumptions of perfect information and rationality, citing behavioral findings such as loss aversion. Much modern macroeconomic theory is built on microfoundations, especially after the Lucas critique.

Laboratory instrument used to examine objects too small to be seen by the naked eye. The science of investigating small structures with one is called microscopy. Microscopes may be grouped by how they interact with a sample: by sending light or electrons through or onto it, by detecting photon emissions from it, or by scanning its surface with a probe. The most common, and first invented, is the [[Optical microscope]], which uses [[Lens|lenses]] to refract visible [[Light|light]] to form an observable image. Other major types are the fluorescence, [[Electron microscope|electron]], and scanning probe microscopes.

Simple microscopes date to the widespread use of lenses in eyeglasses in the 13th century. Compound microscopes, which combine an objective lens near the specimen with an eyepiece, appeared in Europe around 1620. The inventor is unknown, though Dutch spectacle makers and Cornelis Drebbel have been credited. [[Galileo Galilei]] built his own improved version after seeing Drebbel's instrument in Rome in 1624, and the name *microscopio* was coined by Giovanni Faber in 1625.

Microscopes were largely a novelty until the 1660s and 1670s, when naturalists began using them to study biology. [[Robert Hooke]]'s *Micrographia* (1665) had a huge impact. [[Antonie van Leeuwenhoek]] reached up to 300 times magnification with a single ball lens, rediscovered [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]], and reported micro-organisms on October 9, 1676. In 1893 August Köhler developed Köhler illumination, central to reaching the resolution limits of the light microscope. Frits Zernike's phase contrast (1953) and Georges Nomarski's differential interference contrast (1955) allowed imaging of unstained, transparent samples.

Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built the first prototype electron microscope, a transmission type, in 1931. It uses electrons instead of light and electromagnets in place of glass lenses, allowing much higher resolution.

Period of European history lasting approximately from the 5th to the late 15th centuries, also called the medieval period. It is the middle of the three traditional divisions of Western history, between [[Classical antiquity]] and the modern period, and is itself subdivided into the Early, High, and Late Middle Ages.

The era began with the [[Fall of the Western Roman Empire]] and migrations of Germanic peoples, who formed new kingdoms. In the 7th century North Africa and the Middle East, once Byzantine, came under the [[Umayyad Caliphate]]. The Franks under the Carolingians briefly built an empire that succumbed to civil wars and invasions by Vikings, Magyars, and Saracens.

During the High Middle Ages, beginning after 1000, population grew as technological and agricultural innovations allowed trade to flourish. Society was organized through manorialism and [[Feudalism]]. The East–West Schism of 1054 divided the Christian church, and the [[Crusades]], first preached in 1095, were attempts by Western Christians to regain the Holy Land from Muslims. Achievements near the period's end include the theology of [[Thomas Aquinas]], the paintings of Giotto, the poetry of Dante and Chaucer, and Gothic cathedrals such as Chartres.

The Late Middle Ages brought famine, plague, and war; between 1347 and 1350 the [[Black Death]] killed about a third of Europeans.

The term first appears in Latin in 1469 as *media tempestas*. [[Petrarch]] regarded the post-Roman centuries as "dark" compared with classical antiquity, a view some historians challenge, citing continuity in legal traditions, technology, and monastic preservation of classical texts. Christoph Cellarius made the ancient–medieval–modern division standard in the 17th century.

Geopolitical region generally defined as all of Egypt and all of West Asia except the Caucasus. It roughly corresponds to what Western Europe historically called the Near East. It follows political borders rather than continental ones, so it includes East Thrace as part of Turkey. The term has grown prominent since the early 20th century, but its definition is vague and changing; related concepts such as "Middle East and North Africa" and "Greater Middle East" extend it to include most Muslim-majority countries.

Thirteen of its 18 countries belong to the [[Arab world]]. The most populous are Egypt, Iran, and Turkey, and Saudi Arabia is the largest by area. [[Arabs]] are the most widespread ethnic group, followed by Turks, Persians, Kurds, Jews, and Assyrians. Major geographical features include the Arabian Peninsula, [[Anatolia]], the Levant and [[Mesopotamia]] (which together form the [[Fertile Crescent]]), and the Iranian plateau.

Located at the intersection of Africa, Europe, and Asia, the region was the first outside Africa settled by modern humans and the first in which writing systems were developed. All of the core [[Abrahamic religions]], Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, originated there and have their holiest sites there.

Most of the region is hot and arid, especially the Arabian and Egyptian areas. Major rivers, including the Nile, Tigris, Euphrates, and Jordan, support agriculture. The Levantine coast and most of Turkey have a temperate Mediterranean climate. The Gulf Arab states along the [[Persian Gulf]] hold vast reserves of petroleum, which has influenced regional politics. Because of its aridity and dependence on the fossil fuel industry, the region is among the most vulnerable to climate change and water scarcity.

Spanish novelist, poet, playwright, and soldier. He is best known for the two-part [[Novel]] *[[Don Quixote]]*, widely regarded as the first modern novel and often labeled the "best book of all time" by many authors. His reputation as the greatest writer in the Spanish language is reflected in the common description of Spanish as "the language of Cervantes."

Born in Alcalá de Henares to a surgeon father, he spent much of his life in relative poverty and obscurity, and many of his early works were lost. In 1569 he was forced to leave Spain for [[Rome]], where he worked in a cardinal's household. In 1570 he enlisted in a Spanish Navy infantry regiment and was badly wounded at the Battle of Lepanto in October 1571, losing the use of his left arm and hand. He served as a soldier until 1575, when Barbary pirates captured him. After five years in captivity in [[Algiers]], he was ransomed in 1580 and returned to [[Madrid]].

His first significant novel, *La Galatea*, appeared in 1585, while he worked as a purchasing agent and later as a government tax collector; he was imprisoned in 1597 over fiscal irregularities. Part One of *Don Quixote*, a parody of chivalric romances, was published in 1605 and Part Two in 1615. His other works include the 12 *Novelas ejemplares* (*Exemplary Novels*), the long poem *Viaje del Parnaso* (*Journey to Parnassus*), and *Ocho comedias y ocho entremeses* (*Eight Plays and Eight Interludes*). His final novel, *Los trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda* (*The Travails of Persiles and Sigismunda*), was published posthumously in 1617. He was buried in the Convento de las Trinitarias Descalzas in Madrid.

Heavily armed, highly organized force primarily intended for warfare, also called the armed forces. A military is typically authorized and maintained by a [[Sovereign state]], and its members are identifiable by a distinct uniform. It may comprise one or more branches, such as an [[Army]], [[Navy]], [[Air force]], space force, marines, or coast guard. Its main task is usually defined as defending the state and its interests against external armed threats. In technical usage, a distinction is sometimes made in which a country's armed forces may also include paramilitary forces such as armed police.

Beyond warfare, militaries may be employed in other sanctioned and non-sanctioned functions within the state, including internal security, crowd control, emergency services, reconstruction, and ceremonies. A nation's military may function as a discrete social [[Subculture]], with dedicated infrastructure such as housing, schools, utilities, logistics, hospitals, legal services, food production, finance, and banking.

The profession of soldiering is older than recorded history. Images from [[Classical antiquity]] portray the feats of military leaders, and the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BC features in bas-relief monuments from the reign of Ramses II. The first emperor of a unified China, [[Qin Shi Huang]], created the [[Terracotta Army]] to represent his military might.

Militaries evolved from ad hoc tribal groups into structured organizations by antiquity, and professional standing armies emerged prominently in Europe from the 16th to 18th centuries. Core functions today include deterring potential aggressors, projecting power, and achieving superiority in battle. One analysis of engagements from 1600 to 1973 found that numerical advantage, leadership quality, and unit cohesion were decisive, more so than technology alone. Recurring controversies include coups in unstable states and debates over procurement inefficiencies.

Study of armed conflict in human history and its impact on societies, cultures, and economies, together with the resulting changes in local and international relationships. It examines the organization of armed forces, strategic and tactical developments, and the broader social contexts of conflict, treating [[War]] as a driver of technological innovation, state formation, and geopolitical change.

Its essential subjects are the causes of war, the social and cultural foundations of the forces involved, military doctrine on each side, logistics, leadership, technology, strategy, and tactics, and how these changed over time. Just war theory, by contrast, explores the moral dimensions of warfare and seeks to establish a doctrine of military ethics that limits war's destructive reality. Defining conflicts include the Assyrian conquests, Roman expansions, Mongol invasions, and the World Wars.

Military history is taught at academies and service schools as an applied field, because commands aim to prevent past errors and improve performance by training commanders to recognize historical parallels. The Combat Studies Institute, when certifying instructors, deemphasizes rote memorization of detail in favor of themes and context relevant to current and future conflict, under the motto "Past is Prologue."

The discipline changes with military forces, notably during the Industrial Revolution and the nuclear and information ages. The Revolution in Military Affairs (RMA) is a concept that tries to explain how emerging technologies, such as gunpowder, have shaped warfare, highlighting short outbursts of rapid change followed by periods of relative stability. Within the field, debate continues between "operational" military history and a "new" military history that emphasizes cultural and social factors; critics of the latter argue that it dilutes attention to combat outcomes.

Usually white liquid food produced by the mammary glands of lactating mammals. It is the primary source of nutrition for young mammals before they can digest solid food. It is an emulsion of fat globules in a watery solution of proteins, carbohydrates (mainly [[Lactose]]), minerals, and vitamins. Bovine milk provides approximately 3.3 grams of protein per 100 milliliters, along with 3.7% fat, 4.8% lactose, and nutrients such as [[Calcium]] and vitamin D. The first milk, colostrum, contains antibodies that strengthen the immune system.

As an agricultural product, milk is collected from farm animals, mostly [[Cattle]], on a [[Dairy]]. Humans use it as a drink and as the base ingredient of dairy products. More than six billion people worldwide consume milk and milk products. In 2011, dairy farms produced around 730 million tonnes of milk from 260 million dairy cows; global production reached 965.7 million tonnes in 2023. [[India]] is the world's largest producer and the leading exporter of skimmed milk powder, while New Zealand, Germany, and the Netherlands are the largest exporters of milk products.

Adult digestion of milk depends on lactase persistence; lactose-intolerant people have trouble digesting lactose, and the condition limits digestibility for roughly two-thirds of adults globally. [[Pasteurization]] reduces pathogens, though advocates of raw milk cite retained enzymes. Cohort studies link moderate dairy intake to greater bone mineral density and lower risks of [[Colorectal cancer]], while evidence for prostate cancer risk at high intakes is mixed. Health authorities consider dairy beneficial but not essential, since its nutrients are available from other sources, including fortified plant-based milks.

[[Barred spiral galaxy]] that includes the [[Solar System]]; also called the Milky Way Galaxy or simply the Galaxy. The name describes its appearance from Earth: a hazy band of light in the night sky formed by stars in other arms of the galaxy, too distant to be distinguished individually by the naked eye.

[[Galileo Galilei]] first resolved the band into individual stars with his telescope in 1610. Until the early 1920s most astronomers thought it contained all the stars in the universe. After the 1920 Great Debate between Harlow Shapley and Heber Doust Curtis, observations by [[Edwin Hubble]] in 1923 showed it to be only one of many galaxies.

The galaxy has a D25 isophotal diameter estimated at 26.8 ± 1.1 kiloparsecs (87,400 ± 3,600 light-years), and is surrounded by a dark matter area whose total diameter may approach 613 kpc (2 million light-years). The stars in the innermost 10,000 light-years form a bulge, from which the bar radiates. At the center is the intense radio source [[Sagittarius A*]], a supermassive black hole with a mass of 4.100 (±0.034) million solar masses. It is estimated to contain 100–400 billion stars. Its total mass, including [[Dark matter]], is estimated at 1.5 trillion solar masses.

The galaxy is estimated to have formed around 13.6 billion years ago and has grown through mergers with smaller galaxies. The Solar System lies on the inner edge of the Orion Arm, about 27,000 light-years (8.3 kpc) from the Galactic Center, and takes about 240 million years to orbit it. The Milky Way has several satellite galaxies and belongs to the [[Local Group]], part of the Virgo Supercluster, itself a component of the [[Laniakea Supercluster]].
